vi
ABSTRACT
Western cultures have subjugated nature to mankind, depleted her resources, and polluted
the natural world in the name of growth and economic development. The superiority of man and
his domination of the environment has ushered in a new geological and anthropogenic epoch, an
unprecedented period in planetary history, where the exploitation of natural resources and living
beings is the norm. This thesis examines a spectrum of human-nature relationships and explores
the work of cultural theorists and philosophers who examine more intimate connections to the
natural environment. Using these theorists of the human-nature relationship, I propose a criticism
of contemporary approaches to architectural design that cite biomimicry as a method that looks
to nature as a mentor with the primary design goal of efficiency in performance and greater
exploitative economic productivity. As it stands, biomimesis focuses on three main themes:
organism, behavior, and ecosystem. That is to say, biomimicry proposes design innovation while
inspired by nature, this is nature being utilized for goals shaped by Western developmental aims;
whereas, in this thesis, I suggest that nature should be treated as an asset to be protected, and a
depository of wisdom that exceeds any designer’s enthusiasm for efficiency or productivity. This
thesis thus explores the capabilities of biomimicry beyond its contemporary limits, using the
themes of organism, behavior and ecosystem, to reinterpret the architectural medium and its
design practices in the form of a dichotomic reciprocity. In my position, the term dichotomic
reciprocity in this context refers to both the relationship between contrasting agents (nature and
the designer), as well as the capacity for intervention within this relationship to employ a
framework of affective appreciation into the culture of today.

1
CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
Context
Humanity has exhibited exemplary capacity in adapting to unfavorable conditions. Some
historians suggest that this capacity is within human prehistoric animalistic instincts and the
process of evolutionary selection has granted us this ability. Others suggest that it is simply
through innovation that we have advanced. Nevertheless, one key factor that has oftentimes been
omitted, is humanity’s dependence on nature and human’s attempt to establish dominion over
nature. The result is that Western cultures have subjugated nature to man, depleted her resources,
and polluted the natural world. Due to the myriad of cultures and experiences throughout the
world and history, this preeminent relationship between humans and nature is complex but it is
also neglected by designers. An interpretation of our hegemonistic act may arise from a belief in
human distinction in the Western culture of Judeo-Christian tradition (Williams, 2010), that
humans are created under the image of God, and are not animals nor living plants but a distinct
and superior entity to the rest of the natural world, thus giving humans the “authority” to claim
dominance over nature (Hendy, Glosik and Okech, 2005). The progression of this humancentered
hubris has led to detrimental damages to the natural world. It is thus becoming apparent that this
obdurate behavior of superiority must be a focus of concern. Historically, humankind has been
nurtured by planet earth and its diversities of nonhuman entities. They formed an entente with
other forms of flora and fauna. Gradually, a series of expansive “social and cultural
transformations [transpiring] over time and geographical areas” (Harrison, 2018, p. 58)
reoriented the way humans perceived the relationship with nature. Through cultural and
technological development, humans attained a form of consciousness that set us apart from other
species. Continuous industrialization changed a scenario of cohabitation. In the wake of

2
modernization and advancement, humans now officially live in a new geological and
anthropogenic epoch, an unprecedented period in planetary history that justifies domination and
exploitation as a normative. Humans have disrupted Earth and its natural processes, more than all
other forces of nature homogenized. They have climate change, caused extinctions, introduced
invasive species; as according to the Anthropocene Project; technofossils, anthroturbation,
terraforming of land, and redirection of water are only a fraction of the indelible human signature
(Burtynsky, 2017). Humanity’s action of dominance has forced nature to an ever more
vulnerable position and in the paradigm of continuous growth for urban centers, modernization
and technological advancements; this encroachment has created an “invisible” barrier between
man and nature.
Dichotomic reciprocity
Thus, as human civilization progressed at an exponential rate, a predicament arose: The
realization of environmental threats, palpable or probable, to our quality of life. While the notion
of sustainable development is not a relatively new notion, it was revived with the Brundtland
Report was released by the United Nation in 1987. The most accurate definition at the time that
was widely accepted and recognized even up to this day, is that “sustainable development is
development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future
generations to meet their own needs'' (Brundtland, 1987, p. 41). This report also establishes two
key concepts; [1] “the concept of ‘needs’ - in particular, the essential needs of the world’s poor,
to which overriding priority should be given” and [2] “the idea of limitations imposed by the
state of technology and social organization on the environment’s ability to meet present and
future needs.” (Brundtland, 1987, p.41) An ever-growing amount of discourse explores the
multitude of theoretical and methodological approaches of mitigating further disturbance caused
upon the ecosystem. The formation of the modern world, with subjugation as the normative has

3
shaped the environment in disruptive ways, creating what Ruddick referred to as a “destabilizing
moment” (Ruddick, 2010) wherein the balanced construct of the environment is thrown into
disarray (also illustrating Deleuze’s ‘the often-invisible terrain of life’ (Deleuze, 1994)). In order
to reform this association of the ‘negative inseparableness’, this thesis thus envisions how an
architectural discourse could assist in inviting a revision of a cultural tradition of alienation
through a model of dichotomic reciprocity. In order to do so, this thesis will draw from various
theorists and philosophers’ work who advocate for a newly defined culture, with an effort to
rekindle the appreciative attribution for nature. In what follows, I consider the practice of
biomimesis as initiated by the Biomimicry Institute and founder Janine Benyus. Architecturally
speaking, the built environment is the largest contributor that generates negative effects on
nature. Therefore, it comes as no surprise that architecture should be at the forefront of the
discussion on sustainable development. In most approaches, the attempt to address the concern
usually revolves around a generalized range of designs that optimizes efficiency, utilizing
materials that are durable and recyclable, or even what is now labeled as “green architecture”.
However, the effort in addressing sustainable concern on an ecological ethics level is
mortifyingly minuscule. In any case, one could argue that under the broad definition of
ecological architecture, it is identified that architects do design with the environment in mind.
The argument this thesis makes is that while there are claims that the environment is accounted
for, there is a dimension that is lacking in ecological architecture to develop a more intimate
standpoint. The understanding of ecological architecture and the movement of ‘green buildings’
are very much still in favor of humans as opposed to conviviality and co-existence. Nevertheless,
favorable conditions could still be produced and could be made tangible if design approaches
were implemented suitably with nature in mind and could invite humans to consider what could
be a more intimate and convivial co-existence.

4
Hence, our relationship with nature is one that needs to be reassessed. The proposal to
analyze biomimesis is appropriate in exploring the notion of a bio-integration between the
differences in human and nature. As civilization across the globe races towards identifying new
innovations and frontiers, designers and engineers sought a return to nature to seek out adaptive
solutions for performance-based problems within architecture. In many cases, the results are
discussions on how to make buildings highly efficient, more durable and require less energy or
fewer materials. Relating it back to the premise thus far, however, there has been little to no
exploration for how a more intimate relationship with nature can be perceived in green design in
general or in biomimetic architecture when the lens through which we see the value of nature is
one still of the industrial era with its focus on efficiency and control. There has not even been
much exploration about how through nature’s mentoring we could reevaluate our tendencies to
dominate nonhuman species. Therefore, by exploring biomimesis in this way, it opens up the
capabilities for biomimetic architecture to reach beyond its contemporary limits. Instead of the
intervention in the dynamics of evolutionary development to “reshape organisms into tools for
human convenience and profits'' (Coates, 2010 p. 45), this thesis looks into expanding the
understanding to include nature’s ingenuity to improve re-connectivity with nature and to
ameliorate the existing “abusive” culture into one that factors into it an affective framework of
relationship with nature. Ultimately, the proposed reinterpretation of biomimesis chooses to be
perceived as an approach that brings together often detached or disconnected worlds, nature and
technology, life and design. Baumesiter, Tocke, Dwyer, Ritters, and Benyus, in their paper,
suggest: “At its most practical, biomimicry is a way to seek sustainable solutions by borrowing
life’s blueprint, chemical recipes and ecosystem strategies. At its most transformative, biomimicry
connects us in ways that integrate human species into the natural processes of Earth” (Baumesiter,
Tocke, Dwyer, Ritters, Benyus, 2013). This thesis thus seeks to question how biomimesis can help

5
architects and engineers develop a more intimate relationship between humans and non-human
species, specifically with the utilization of architecture as the medium, as well as hypothesizing on
how might we formulate a solution of sharing the planet with nonhuman subjects to treat them
justly through a model of dichotomic reciprocity?
Lastly, and in addition to literature review and case study research this thesis takes an
approach into reconceptualizing biomimesis in a design strategy. While biomimesis excels in
inspiring strategies and solutions on an efficiency basis, the intent is to explore in design how
biomimesis could invite the reconditioning of an exploitative culture into one that validates a
panarchy with nonhuman species. By doing so, the exploitative culture that exists would be
replaced with a tendency to view nature not as a commodity, but rather a source of knowledge
and mentor in relationships. Fortuitously, while the COVID-19 pandemic is a devastating ordeal,
it has given us a necessary pause in time to re-evaluate these concerns and to drastically change
human’s perspective on the relationship with nature that has been tainted.
Biomimicry, and a glimpse of what is to come: how can we live together?
The current model with which humans live in, is unsustainable. Statistically speaking, the
human population has made an exponential increase since achieving 1 billion individuals in the
1800s to eventually reaching 4 billion in the year 1975. As sectors of technology and medicine
have made progressive advancements and productivity, the statistics of population unsurprisingly
escalated to an approximation of 8 billion in the year 2020. Analytical projections predict that the
human population could potentially hit anywhere between 9 to 15 billion people by the year
2050. While this “population explosion” is often celebrated as a great achievement in planetary
history, a devastating consequence of this Anthropocene epoch (an age where humans dominate
over all planetary conditions) is also a deleterious increase in domination over nature. Evidently,

6
leading towards the exploitation of natural resources with no bound, thus ultimately being
threatened into extinction. Notwithstanding the differences in biodiversity, species distribution,
climate and consumption pattern, it is apparent that the density of human pressure is indefinitely
the key factor towards environmental threats. Inasmuch of human’s demand on natural resources,
we are exceeding the Earth’s capacity to regenerate quickly enough to sustain itself. Humanity
has exploited nature’s generosity to its absolute limits. To put it into perspective, the 2020
version of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s (IUCN) Red List of Threatened
Species indicates that nearly a quarter of the total amount of species being evaluated (32,441
species out of 120,372 species) are currently threatened with extinction. Jeffrey McKee, a
physical anthropologist at the Ohio State University suggests that further damages and threats
could prevail if other species replicate the same patterns as mammals and birds en masse. In
order to maintain a sustainable model, the ecological footprint would need to meet an
approximation of 1.7 times the level of biocapacity (Figure 1). What this reveal in terms of a
sustainable model is that we would require ‘1.7 Earth’ to generate enough resources for
humanity. (Global Biodiversity Outlook, 2020, p. 48)
When looking back at the overall population, human civilization stands at a whopping 8
billion people collectively, which makes up but a small percentage of one one-hundredth (0.01%)
of the entire biomass, yet they instinctively contributed to 83% of all wild mammal’s
extinction.(Figure 2) An even more alarming study compiled by Damian Carrington, an
environmental editor of The Guardian - a British news website, identified and revealed that only
4% of the existing biomass can be considered as mammals of wildlife, while the remaining
percentage is divided between livestock (60%) and humans (36%).

From the years 1986 to 2018 alone, Clare Perry, a UK Environmental Investigator stated
that three countries alone had contributed to the extermination of roughly 40,000 great whales as
a result of whaling. (International Whaling Commission, 2018). By the end of the year 2019,
Eimear Nic Lughadha, a senior research leader at RBG Kew (Royal Botanic Garden) reported
that since 1750 to 2019, an estimate of 571 plant species have been completely wiped off the

8
surface of the earth (Royal Botanic Garden, 2019). Based on a report done by IUCN, at least
40% of wild plants are threatened by extinction. Human invasion on the ecologically rich habitat
is slowly resulting into what experts are referring to as a potential “sixth mass extinction” to
occur in Earth’s annals (IUCN, 2021). The reciprocation relationship between humans and
nonhumans is imbalanced.
Based on what is present and can be grasped in architecture, design movements from the
past were usually driven to “mechanical and separation mentality” (Brajovic, 2020). What this
means is that the built environment after the industrial revolution was designed only for humans
(although it did eventually consider small, domesticated nonhumans) and were made into an
“operational apparatus for living” that would simultaneously become the largest contributor for
negative effects on the ecosystem services. Although architectural scholars and theorists are in
constant flux at addressing the issues with methods and solutions, what is often omitted or
dismissed in that process is the idea of a reconceptualization for an intimate relationship with
nature. Relative to the current situation of the COVID-19 pandemic, a conversation that was
brought forward by Hashim Sarkis, the 17th Architectural Exhibition curator of La Biennale di
Venezia conveyed a strong interest in this discord amongst human and nonhuman lifeforms.
Sarkis’ theme opened up an “existential portal for humanity” (La Biennale di Venezia, 2020). To
Sarkis, the dilemma can be viewed from both a social and political stance, as well as a spatial
one. It is due to rapid unpredictable transformations within social norms, political polarization,
climatic changes as well as inequalities that urgently questions the way we live at differing
scales. This impending question is without a doubt more prevailing in recent years. As a matter
of fact, several philosophies of Luce Irigaray contemplate similar ethical dispositions as well.
Irigaray’s fundamental inquisition on “How can we live in a lasting way together?” describes an

9
idea of being two; a mode of growing together or the closeness with others in an equitable
relationship (Irigaray, 2004 pp. 123-133). The notion of re-formulating the concept of the
singularity could also then be applied into the conquest for a symbiotic relationship towards
nature. As such, this thesis draws inspiration from both Sarkis’s theme, as well as with Irigaray’s
discord on sexuate differences, and proposes a derivative which conclusively extends to “How
can we accommodate for a model of dichotomic reciprocity?”
Ironically, while the world has been in disarray, the conditions imposed by the COVID19
pandemic has re-enabled a transition from the narrative of an “inter-subjective reality - where a
binary of humans and nature dialectic was aestheticized by romantic existentialism” (Brajovic,
2020), to a culture that starts to understand both the radical and empirical need, as well as an
appreciation for “solidarity with nonhuman species” (Morton, 2017). Charles Eisenstein states:
“COVID-19 is like a rehab intervention that breaks the addictive hold of normality”. Throughout
the living days of isolative quarantining, what seems to have developed is a subtle re-connection
back with nature (although not to a desired level yet), as observable by extreme reduction of
pollution and a decrease in international consumption. Remarkably in accordance with the
pandemic, the slowdown of the global economy helped in reducing the estimated figure of the
ecological footprint that would have needed to meet an approximation of 1.7 times the level of
biocapacity. (Global Biodiversity Outlook, 2020). Therefore, the global state is in a dire need of a
paradigm shift on the perception, in hopes to rediscover a coexisting society with nonhuman
species. The expectations as a result of this community; as Luce Irigaray puts it, has the potential
to open up avenues of innovative solutions in contemporary practice and cultural changes, not to
mention an interrelated network of life. It is paramount to remember that this planet is very much
a living organism, reliant on interminable dependence with one another. In reality, none of this

10
should come across as new knowledge to indigeneity or “ancestral apprehension”. Information as
such had always been expressed by people of indigenous background, even to this day.
What seems to become apparent from the discussions above is an intentional and
necessary diverge from a manipulative behavior to a multifaceted comity that stimulates an
engagement which performs appropriately and sustainably with nature. This could be made
possible by potentially considering certain characteristics of the salutogenesis model that was
proposed by sociologist Aaron Antonovsky. While salutogenic designs are usually implemented
in medical sectors, the idea of the models construct of ‘coherence’ as an orientation over
cognition (Mittelmark and Bauer, 2016) can be extracted and carried into increasing societal and
ecological synergy. This in return would aid in the awareness of sensitivity to ecological
conditions, and to facilitate an order from a detached perspective of the separation culture to a
more holistic culture - as a part of nature. To familiarize the validity of a panarchic culture with
nonhuman species in biomimetic architecture, Philip Ivanhoe’s Oneness hypothesis (Ivanhoe,
2015) would also become relevant in resuscitating the relationship. As rationalized, the Oneness
hypothesis substantiates “connections that conduce to the health, benefit, and improvement of
both individuals and the larger whole of which they are parts.” (Ivanhoe, 2018). As a matter of
fact, the oneness hypothesis is interpreted differently in varieties of writing and industries,
however what is explored in this thesis is human dependence on nonhuman species - that one’s
flourishment and contentment is bounded with the profound and inseparable well-being of others
(Flanagan, 2019). If this becomes accepted, the architectural view or notion is of an ecological
appreciative framework focused on social and ethical change. The Oneness hypothesis will be
further elaborated in later sections. Architecturally speaking, based on the finite numbers of
approaches to sustainable development, I posit that biomimetic architecture, if incorporated
correctly, could potentially provoke a greater dialogue.
